title: How close is the sacred?
hookLine: the Aitareya and the Qur'an on how near the sacred is
carry: Brahman is as near as your own knowing
tomorrow: the Aitareya ends by saying one thing twice. what is it?
last: EVEN A WANT IS A NAME OF THE KNOWING.

cards: Two fingers on the side of the neck after a run, counting the pulse. It's about as close as anything gets: under the skin, never off duty.
Plenty of pictures put the sacred far away, above the clouds, at the end of a long road. So, one question today. How close is it?
The Aitareya Upanishad has an answer. So does a neighbor, and it reaches for that same pulse.

teach.b: The Aitareya's answer is the closest thing there is. The knowing by which you see this room, hear this voice, want and remember: that, it says, is Brahman. Prajnanam brahma.
Not reached by travel, not waiting at the end of a road. Already doing the seeing. The Qur'an, the scripture of Islam, gives its own answer to how close, and it uses the body too.

teach.h: THE QUR'AN: NEARER THAN THE JUGULAR VEIN.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation, the voice Muslims understand as God's says: "We verily created man and We know what his soul whispereth to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein."
Here's what the two share. Neither puts the sacred far off. Each reaches for the nearest thing a person has, the knowing behind the eyes, the vein in the neck, and says: closer than that.
And here's the honest difference. In the Qur'an, the one who is near is God, the Creator, who made the person and knows even the soul's whisper, and the person is not God.

teach.h: DIFFERENT: MAKER NEAR, OR KNOWER AS BRAHMAN.
teach.b: In the Aitareya, as Advaita reads it, the knowing itself is Brahman; as Ramanuja reads it, Brahman is the inner self of the one who knows.
So two pictures of nearness: a Maker closer than your own pulse, and a reality that is, or dwells in, your own knowing. Each tradition keeps its own, and both refuse to call the sacred far away.

how: In Vedanta study, prajnanam brahma is reflected on as pointing to the knowing within; in Islam the Qur'an is recited as God's word, and Surah Qaf (50:16) speaks of God being nearer than the jugular vein.

four signs that the sacred is far away

games.q: how close? two answers. tap the pairs.
p: the sacred is not far off
a Maker near, or the knowing itself

s: the Upanishads picture the sacred as far away, at the end of a long road
the Aitareya says the knowing that's doing the seeing is Brahman: as near as it gets.
the Qur'an says God is nearer to a person than the jugular vein
Qur'an 50:16, in Pickthall's translation: nearer to him than his jugular vein.
the Qur'an and the Aitareya say exactly the same thing
both say near. in the Qur'an God the Creator is near and the person is not God; the Aitareya calls the knowing itself Brahman.

games.q: at dinner someone says: 'all religions really say the same thing: you are God.' you've just read the Aitareya and the Qur'an side by side. what's fair?
o: they share 'very near'; they differ on whether the knower is God. say both.
agree: every tradition teaches that each person is God.
disagree: those two books share nothing at all.
games.why: both refuse to put the sacred far off. in the Qur'an the Creator is nearer than the jugular vein; in the Aitareya the knowing itself is Brahman. 'all religions say you are God' isn't neutral.

practice: Close your eyes. Rest two fingers lightly on your wrist or the side of your neck until you find the pulse. Stay with it, beat after beat, and notice that something is knowing each beat as it comes.

wordCard.voice: The four mahavakyas, and prajnanam brahma's answer to how close: the knowing that's already doing the seeing.

orig.note: Sanskrit prajnanam, the knowing: the first word of the Aitareya's great saying.

carryVoice: The line to keep: Brahman is as near as your own knowing, as near as whoever is listening. Until tomorrow.
